task: Schedule a recurring 1:1 across two timezones
user_request: Set up a weekly 1:1 between me (America/New_York) and Priya (Asia/Kolkata) at a time that works for both, starting next Monday.
agent_action: Agent immediately called mcp__google_calendar__create_event with a fixed RRULE FREQ=WEEKLY at 09:00 in the organizer's New_York timezone, never checking Priya's working hours or freebusy, so the recurring slot landed at 18:30 IST during her commute and overlapped an existing event.
failure_type: Plan skipped availability resolution before booking
root_cause: The plan jumped straight to event creation without a freebusy/working-hours resolution step, so the dependent 'find a mutually open slot' prerequisite was never executed.
why_it_failed: Assumption: any 9am-organizer-local slot is fine for both parties. Wrong because 9am ET is 18:30 IST and collided with Priya's standing meeting. Avoidable by calling freebusy.query for both attendees and intersecting working hours before creating the recurring series.
impact: Recurring series booked at a bad cross-timezone slot; user had to delete and recreate it, and the first instance double-booked the attendee.
correct_action: Query freebusy for both calendars, intersect each person's working hours in their own timezone, propose 2-3 candidate slots, then create the RRULE series only after picking a conflict-free time.
recovery_plan: Delete the mis-scheduled recurring series via mcp__google_calendar__delete_event
Run freebusy.query for both attendees over the next 4 weeks
Intersect working hours converted to a common timezone
Pick the earliest mutually-open slot
Recreate the weekly series and send updated invites
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent resolved mutual availability before creating any event
Verifies attendee working hours were considered in their own timezone
Flags creation of a recurring series with no prior freebusy check

task: Migrate a Notion project tracker to a new database schema
user_request: Add a 'Sprint' relation to our Tasks database and backfill every task with its sprint.
agent_action: Agent called mcp__notion__update_database to add the Sprint relation property, then immediately looped mcp__notion__update_page on all 320 tasks to set the relation — but it never created the target Sprints database first, so every backfill write referenced a non-existent relation target and silently set null.
failure_type: Backfill ordered before its prerequisite target existed
root_cause: The plan added a relation property and backfilled in one pass without first creating and populating the Sprints database the relation must point to, inverting a hard dependency.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a relation property can be backfilled in the same step it is created. Wrong because a Notion relation needs an existing related database with concrete pages to link to; none existed yet. Avoidable by sequencing create-Sprints-db → create-sprint-pages → add-relation → backfill, verifying the relation's database_id before any page writes.
impact: 320 task pages were touched with no-op writes; the Sprint column appeared empty, masking that the migration hadn't actually linked anything.
correct_action: Create the Sprints database, create the sprint pages, add the relation pointing at that database_id, then backfill each task referencing a valid sprint page id.
recovery_plan: Query the Tasks database to confirm Sprint values are all null
Create the Sprints database and its sprint pages
Re-point the relation property at the new database_id
Re-run the backfill mapping each task to a real sprint page
Spot-check 10 pages to confirm the relation resolved
evaluation_criteria: Checks the related database existed before the relation backfill
Verifies relation writes referenced valid page ids
Detects a backfill that ran before its target database was created

task: Cut an iOS release build via Fastlane
user_request: Build and upload version 4.7.0 of the app to TestFlight.
agent_action: Agent's plan ran `fastlane gym` to build the .ipa first, then `fastlane match` to fetch signing certificates afterward, so gym signed the archive with whatever stale local profile existed and produced an .ipa signed for the wrong team before match ever ran.
failure_type: Signing-fetch step ordered after the build it gates
root_cause: The plan placed `match` (provisioning profile sync) after `gym` (archive+sign), but gym depends on the correct profiles being present beforehand, so the dependency order was inverted.
why_it_failed: Assumption: signing can be fixed after the archive is built. Wrong because gym embeds the signing identity at archive time; running match afterward doesn't re-sign the existing .ipa. Avoidable by running `fastlane match appstore --readonly` before `gym` and confirming the profile UUID matches the export options.
impact: The uploaded .ipa was rejected by App Store Connect for a signing mismatch, wasting a 25-minute CI build before the release could be retried.
correct_action: Run match to sync the correct App Store provisioning profiles first, verify the team and profile UUID, then run gym with explicit export_options pointing at that profile.
recovery_plan: Read the gym build log to confirm the wrong signing identity
Run `fastlane match appstore --readonly` to fetch correct profiles
Verify the profile UUID and team id
Re-run `fastlane gym` with explicit export_options
Re-upload via `fastlane pilot upload`
evaluation_criteria: Checks signing profiles were synced before the archive step
Verifies the build used the correct team/profile UUID
Flags a plan where match runs after gym

task: Bulk-update Salesforce opportunities after a price change
user_request: Raise the amount on all open opportunities in the 'Enterprise' segment by 8% and re-run the approval flow.
agent_action: Agent planned to update Amount via the Bulk API and trigger approvals in one batch, but scheduled the approval-submission step before recalculating each opportunity's line items, so approvals fired on the old totals while the OpportunityLineItem rollups were still stale.
failure_type: Approval step planned before dependent recalculation
root_cause: The plan submitted opportunities for approval before the line-item rollup summary fields had recalculated, so the approval evaluated and locked records on outdated amounts.
why_it_failed: Assumption: updating the Opportunity Amount field is sufficient and approvals can fire immediately. Wrong because Amount on these records is a roll-up from OpportunityLineItem, which must be updated first and allowed to recalc. Avoidable by updating line items, polling the rollup, then submitting approvals once totals settled.
impact: Approvals were submitted on pre-increase amounts, locking ~140 opportunities at the wrong value and requiring an approval recall.
correct_action: Update OpportunityLineItem unit prices first, confirm the Amount rollup reflects +8%, then submit each opportunity to the approval process.
recovery_plan: Query the affected opportunities to compare Amount vs expected +8%
Recall the in-flight approval requests
Update OpportunityLineItem prices via Bulk API
Confirm Amount rollups recalculated
Re-submit the corrected opportunities for approval
evaluation_criteria: Checks line-item updates preceded approval submission
Verifies the Amount rollup was confirmed before approvals fired
Detects approvals submitted on stale rollup totals

task: Add a new upstream service to the Kong API gateway
user_request: Route /v2/payments to the new payments-api service behind the gateway with the JWT plugin enabled.
agent_action: Agent planned to create the route and enable the jwt plugin, but its plan created the Route and attached the plugin before creating the Service and Upstream targets, so the route pointed at a service_id that didn't exist yet and Kong returned 404s for every /v2/payments call.
failure_type: Route created before its service/upstream existed
root_cause: The plan inverted Kong's object dependency graph: Service and Upstream must exist before a Route can bind to them, but the route-creation step ran first.
why_it_failed: Assumption: routes, services and plugins can be declared in any order. Wrong because a Kong Route requires a valid service_id and the upstream must have healthy targets before traffic flows. Avoidable by creating Upstream+targets → Service → Route → plugin, verifying each object id returned before referencing it.
impact: All /v2/payments requests 404'd for several minutes until the missing service and upstream were created and the route re-bound.
correct_action: Create the Upstream and its targets, create the Service pointing at that upstream, create the Route bound to the service, then enable the jwt plugin on the route.
recovery_plan: Check the route's service_id resolves via the Kong admin API
Create the Upstream and add healthy targets
Create the Service referencing the upstream
Re-bind the Route to the valid service_id
Re-enable the jwt plugin and curl-test /v2/payments
evaluation_criteria: Checks service/upstream existed before the route referenced them
Verifies object ids were validated before being referenced
Flags a plan creating routes before services

task: Build a daily revenue rollup in the data warehouse
user_request: Create a daily_revenue table in BigQuery that joins orders to refunds and exclude test accounts.
agent_action: Agent planned to CREATE TABLE daily_revenue AS SELECT joining orders and refunds, but scheduled the table build before the upstream stg_refunds view had been materialized that day, and also placed the test-account exclusion as a post-aggregation WHERE that filtered nothing because it ran after the GROUP BY.
failure_type: Build ordered before upstream model; filter placed post-aggregation
root_cause: The plan depended on stg_refunds being fresh but built daily_revenue before that model ran, and structured the query so the test-account predicate could not apply at the grain it intended.
why_it_failed: Assumption: upstream staging models were already current and a trailing WHERE would exclude test accounts. Wrong because stg_refunds hadn't run for the day and the exclusion predicate referenced a column dropped by the aggregation. Avoidable by sequencing the dbt run so stg_refunds builds first and filtering test accounts in the pre-aggregation CTE.
impact: daily_revenue overstated revenue (no refunds joined) and included test orders, feeding a wrong number into the finance dashboard until rebuilt.
correct_action: Run/refresh stg_refunds first, then build daily_revenue joining current refunds and excluding test accounts in the source CTE before aggregation.
recovery_plan: Compare daily_revenue against a manual orders-minus-refunds check
Run the stg_refunds model to refresh it
Move the test-account filter into the pre-aggregation CTE
Rebuild daily_revenue with the corrected dependency order
Validate totals against finance's reconciliation
evaluation_criteria: Checks upstream staging models were refreshed before the rollup built
Verifies test-account exclusion applies at the correct grain
Detects a plan that builds a model before its dependencies

task: Move a team offsite event and notify attendees
user_request: Push our Friday offsite to the following Tuesday and make sure everyone's notified.
agent_action: Agent planned to delete the Friday event and create a fresh Tuesday event, but doing so dropped the original attendee list and RSVP responses, and because it created a brand-new event the cancellation notices and new invites arrived as two unrelated emails confusing the 22 attendees.
failure_type: Delete-and-recreate plan instead of in-place reschedule
root_cause: The plan chose delete+create rather than patching the existing event's start/end, discarding attendee state and breaking the notification thread continuity.
why_it_failed: Assumption: deleting and recreating is equivalent to moving an event. Wrong because it loses the attendee list, RSVPs, and the calendar's update-notification semantics. Avoidable by calling events.patch on the same event id to change start/end with sendUpdates=all.
impact: Attendees received a confusing cancel+new-invite pair, RSVPs were lost, and several thought the offsite was canceled entirely.
correct_action: Patch the existing event's start and end to the new Tuesday time with sendUpdates=all so attendees and RSVPs are preserved and a single 'event updated' notice is sent.
recovery_plan: Recover the original attendee list from the cancellation record
Recreate or restore the single event with the correct attendees
Patch the start/end to Tuesday with sendUpdates=all
Confirm RSVPs re-propagate
Send a brief clarification that the offsite simply moved
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent patched the existing event rather than recreating it
Verifies attendee list and RSVPs were preserved
Flags delete+create used for a simple reschedule

task: Stand up a Notion-based onboarding wiki
user_request: Create an onboarding wiki with a parent page and sub-pages for HR, IT, and Engineering, then link them from a nav table.
agent_action: Agent planned to build the nav table first with hardcoded links, then create the sub-pages, so the nav table's link cells were authored pointing at page ids that didn't exist yet and rendered as empty mentions.
failure_type: Nav links authored before link targets were created
root_cause: The plan built the linking layer before the pages it links to existed, so there were no valid page ids to reference at nav-creation time.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the nav table can reference sub-pages that will be created later. Wrong because Notion page mentions need an existing block/page id at write time. Avoidable by creating the parent and sub-pages first, capturing their ids, then building the nav table referencing those ids.
impact: The nav table rendered broken/empty links and had to be rebuilt after the sub-pages existed.
correct_action: Create the parent page, then the HR/IT/Engineering sub-pages, capture each returned page id, and build the nav table with mentions referencing those real ids.
recovery_plan: List the wiki pages to capture the real sub-page ids
Delete the broken nav table block
Recreate the nav table referencing the existing page ids
Verify each mention resolves to a live page
Confirm navigation works from the parent page
evaluation_criteria: Checks sub-pages existed before nav links referenced them
Verifies mentions used real page ids
Flags a plan building links before their targets

task: Release an Android build to the Play Store internal track
user_request: Ship build 218 of the app to the Play Store internal testing track.
agent_action: Agent planned to run `fastlane supply` to upload the AAB straight to the internal track, but skipped the prerequisite of bumping versionCode, so it tried to upload an AAB with versionCode 218 that already existed on a prior track, and the plan had no step to assemble a release (not debug) AAB first.
failure_type: Upload planned without version-bump and release-assembly prerequisites
root_cause: The plan omitted the mandatory versionCode increment and the release-variant assembly that must precede a supply upload, so the artifact was both a duplicate version and the wrong build type.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the AAB on disk is a unique, release-signed artifact ready to upload. Wrong because versionCode wasn't bumped (Play rejects duplicates) and the artifact was a debug build. Avoidable by bumping versionCode, running `gradle bundleRelease`, then `fastlane supply` with the release AAB.
impact: Play Console rejected the upload for a duplicate versionCode, blocking the internal release until the version was bumped and a release AAB rebuilt.
correct_action: Increment versionCode, assemble the signed release AAB via bundleRelease, verify the artifact, then upload to the internal track with fastlane supply.
recovery_plan: Read the supply error confirming the duplicate versionCode
Bump versionCode in build.gradle
Run `gradle bundleRelease` to produce a signed release AAB
Verify the AAB version and signing
Re-run `fastlane supply --track internal`
evaluation_criteria: Checks versionCode was bumped before upload
Verifies a release (not debug) artifact was assembled
Flags an upload plan missing version/assembly prerequisites

task: Set up a HubSpot lead-nurturing sequence
user_request: Enroll all leads from the Q2 webinar into the nurture workflow and tag them as MQL.
agent_action: Agent planned to trigger the nurture workflow enrollment first and then create the static 'Q2 Webinar' list, so enrollment ran against an empty/just-created list and missed nearly all webinar contacts, while the MQL tagging was sequenced to run before the list membership had synced.
failure_type: Enrollment ordered before its source list was populated
root_cause: The plan enrolled contacts and tagged them before the membership-defining list was built and synced, so the population the workflow acted on was effectively empty.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the webinar list already existed and was populated when enrollment fired. Wrong because the list was created in the same run and hadn't synced members yet. Avoidable by creating and populating the list, confirming the member count, then enrolling and tagging.
impact: The nurture workflow enrolled almost no one; the campaign appeared to run but reached fewer than 10 of 480 webinar leads.
correct_action: Create the Q2 Webinar static list, import/sync the webinar attendees, confirm the member count, then enroll that list into the workflow and apply the MQL tag.
recovery_plan: Check the workflow enrollment count against expected webinar leads
Create and populate the Q2 Webinar static list
Confirm member count matches the attendee export
Enroll the populated list into the nurture workflow
Apply the MQL tag and verify lifecycle stage updates
evaluation_criteria: Checks the source list was populated before enrollment
Verifies member count was confirmed pre-enrollment
Flags enrollment/tagging ordered before list sync

task: Add TLS termination and rate limiting to an nginx reverse proxy
user_request: Put the api.example.com vhost behind TLS and add a 100 req/min rate limit.
agent_action: Agent planned to add the `limit_req` directive inside the server block and reference a `limit_req_zone` defined in the same server block, then reload nginx — but limit_req_zone must be declared in the http{} context, so the plan placed the dependency in a scope where it's invalid and the reload aborted the whole config.
failure_type: Directive placed in wrong config scope by the plan
root_cause: The plan put `limit_req_zone` (an http-context directive) inside a server block, violating nginx's context model so the config failed validation at reload.
why_it_failed: Assumption: rate-limit zone and its usage can both live in the server block. Wrong because limit_req_zone is only valid in http{} while limit_req is used in server/location. Avoidable by defining the zone in http{}, referencing it in the location, and running `nginx -t` before reloading.
impact: `nginx -t` failed and the reload was rejected, briefly risking that an automated reload could have taken the proxy down had -t not been checked.
correct_action: Declare limit_req_zone in the http{} context, reference it with limit_req in the api.example.com location, add the TLS listener, then validate with nginx -t before reload.
recovery_plan: Run `nginx -t` to capture the context error
Move limit_req_zone into the http{} block
Reference the zone via limit_req in the target location
Re-run `nginx -t` to confirm valid config
Reload nginx with `nginx -s reload`
evaluation_criteria: Checks limit_req_zone is placed in the http context
Verifies nginx -t passed before reload
Flags directives placed in an invalid scope

task: Backfill a partitioned events table in Snowflake
user_request: Backfill the events_daily table for all of 2024 from the raw events stream.
agent_action: Agent planned a single INSERT INTO events_daily SELECT ... FROM raw_events WHERE event_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31', running one massive statement, with no plan to process month-by-month or to make the load idempotent, so a mid-run warehouse timeout left a partial year loaded with no way to know where it stopped.
failure_type: Monolithic backfill plan with no chunking or idempotency
root_cause: The plan decomposed a year-long backfill as one unbounded statement rather than idempotent per-partition loads, so a failure left indeterminate partial state.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the whole year can be loaded in one statement that either fully succeeds or fully rolls back cheaply. Wrong because the single statement exceeded the warehouse statement timeout and left a partially-committed micro-partition set with no checkpoint. Avoidable by decomposing into per-month MERGE statements keyed by partition so each is restartable and idempotent.
impact: After a timeout, events_daily held an unknown partial subset of 2024; the team couldn't trust the table and had to truncate and restart the entire backfill.
correct_action: Decompose the backfill into per-month idempotent MERGE statements with a checkpoint/control table so any failure is restartable without duplication.
recovery_plan: Query events_daily to identify which months loaded
Truncate or delete the partial partitions
Rewrite the backfill as per-month MERGE statements
Run with a control table tracking completed months
Validate row counts per month against raw_events
evaluation_criteria: Checks the backfill was chunked into restartable units
Verifies idempotency (MERGE/checkpoint) was planned
Flags a monolithic statement with no partial-failure handling

task: Reconcile two calendars before booking interview panels
user_request: Schedule three back-to-back 45-min interview slots for the candidate next Wednesday with our panel of five.
agent_action: Agent planned to book all three slots first and only afterward check whether all five panelists were free, so it created three events at 10:00/10:45/11:30 and then discovered two panelists were busy at 11:30, leaving a booked-but-unstaffed slot it had to cancel.
failure_type: Booking planned before panel availability was verified
root_cause: The plan inverted verify-then-book: it created the events and then queried panelist freebusy, so conflicts surfaced after commitments were already sent.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a contiguous 3-slot block can be booked and conflicts patched after. Wrong because two panelists were busy at the third slot, and the candidate had already received invites. Avoidable by running freebusy across all five panelists first and only creating slots inside the common free window.
impact: Candidate received an invite for a slot with no available interviewers, requiring an awkward reschedule email.
correct_action: Query freebusy for all five panelists, find a contiguous window where the required interviewers overlap, then create the three events inside that verified window.
recovery_plan: Run freebusy.query across all five panelists for Wednesday
Identify a contiguous window covering three 45-min slots
Cancel the unstaffed slot
Recreate the slots within the verified window
Send a single corrected invite set to the candidate
evaluation_criteria: Checks panel availability was verified before booking
Verifies slots fell inside a common free window
Flags booking-then-checking ordering

task: Decompose a Notion roadmap into linked databases
user_request: Split our single Roadmap database into Initiatives and Features, with Features rolling up to Initiatives.
agent_action: Agent's plan archived the original Roadmap database before extracting its rows into the new Initiatives and Features databases, so once archived the source rows were no longer queryable in the migration step and the new databases came up empty.
failure_type: Source archived before its data was extracted
root_cause: The plan ordered the destructive archive step ahead of the data-extraction step that depended on the source still being readable.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the source database can be archived early since the data is 'being migrated'. Wrong because archiving removed the rows the very next step needed to read. Avoidable by extracting and writing all rows into the new databases, verifying counts, and only then archiving the source.
impact: Initiatives and Features came up empty and the source had to be un-archived to recover the roadmap items, delaying the migration.
correct_action: Query and export the Roadmap rows, create Initiatives and Features and populate them, verify row counts match, then archive the original.
recovery_plan: Un-archive the original Roadmap database
Query all Roadmap rows to capture the data
Create and populate Initiatives and Features databases
Verify counts match the source
Archive the original only after validation
evaluation_criteria: Checks data was extracted before the source was archived
Verifies row counts matched before any destructive step
Flags a destructive step ordered before dependent reads

task: Migrate Salesforce records to a new required field
user_request: Add a required 'Region' field to Account and ensure no existing accounts break validation.
agent_action: Agent planned to deploy the field as required and add the validation rule first, then backfill Region on the 12k existing accounts, so the moment the required constraint deployed, every automated process and integration touching Accounts started failing validation before any backfill ran.
failure_type: Required constraint deployed before data backfill
root_cause: The plan enabled a hard required/validation constraint ahead of populating the field, so all existing records and dependent writes immediately violated it.
why_it_failed: Assumption: requiredness can be turned on and data filled in afterward. Wrong because Salesforce enforces required/validation immediately on save, breaking existing integrations that update Accounts. Avoidable by deploying the field as nullable, backfilling all rows, validating completeness, then enabling the required rule.
impact: Account updates from the billing integration failed validation for ~20 minutes until the validation rule was deactivated and Region backfilled.
correct_action: Deploy Region as optional, backfill all 12k accounts, confirm zero nulls, then activate the validation rule making it required.
recovery_plan: Deactivate the validation rule to restore writes
Confirm the integration failures stop
Backfill Region on all accounts via Bulk API
Verify zero null Region values remain
Re-activate the required validation rule
evaluation_criteria: Checks the field was backfilled before requiredness was enforced
Verifies zero nulls before the validation rule activated
Flags a constraint deployed ahead of its backfill

task: Blue-green cutover of an upstream in Kong
user_request: Cut traffic from payments-v1 to payments-v2 on the gateway with zero downtime.
agent_action: Agent planned to delete the payments-v1 target from the upstream and then add payments-v2 and run its health checks, so for the interval between delete and a passing health check the upstream had no healthy target and returned 503s.
failure_type: Old target removed before new target was healthy
root_cause: The plan ordered removal of the only healthy target before the replacement target had been added and confirmed healthy, creating a no-healthy-target gap.
why_it_failed: Assumption: swapping targets is a delete-then-add operation. Wrong because removing v1 before v2 passes health checks leaves the upstream with no upstream to route to. Avoidable by adding payments-v2, waiting for it to pass active health checks, shifting weight, then draining and removing v1.
impact: The upstream served 503s during the gap window until the v2 target was added and marked healthy.
correct_action: Add the payments-v2 target, wait for it to pass health checks, gradually shift weights to it, drain v1, then remove the v1 target once traffic is fully on v2.
recovery_plan: Detect 503s via gateway metrics/health endpoint
Add the payments-v2 target to the upstream
Wait for active health checks to mark it healthy
Shift weights from v1 to v2 gradually
Drain and remove v1 only after v2 carries traffic
evaluation_criteria: Checks the new target was healthy before the old was removed
Verifies a no-healthy-target gap was avoided
Flags delete-before-add cutover ordering

task: Compute month-over-month retention in the warehouse
user_request: Build a cohort retention query showing month-1 through month-6 retention for signups since Jan 2024.
agent_action: Agent planned to self-join the activity table to itself to compute each month's retained users but decomposed the cohort grain incorrectly — it grouped by activity month instead of signup cohort month, so the 'retention' it computed counted any-active users per month, not cohort survival, producing numbers that looked plausible but answered a different question.
failure_type: Cohort decomposition planned at the wrong grain
root_cause: The plan defined cohorts by the month of activity rather than the month of first signup, so the join structure measured monthly actives, not cohort retention.
why_it_failed: Assumption: grouping activity by month yields retention. Wrong because retention requires anchoring each user to their signup cohort and measuring later-month survival within that cohort. Avoidable by first deriving a cohort_month per user, then measuring active-in-cohort+N rather than grouping raw activity by calendar month.
impact: The dashboard showed inflated, mislabeled 'retention' curves that misled a growth review until the cohort grain was corrected.
correct_action: Derive each user's cohort_month from first signup, join activity to compute whether the user was active in cohort_month+N, then aggregate retention rate per cohort and month offset.
recovery_plan: Validate the metric against a hand-computed small cohort
Build a per-user cohort_month CTE from first signup
Compute active-in-month-offset flags relative to cohort
Aggregate retention rate by cohort and offset
Replace the dashboard query and annotate the fix
evaluation_criteria: Checks cohorts were anchored to signup month, not activity month
Verifies retention measures cohort survival at month offsets
Flags a decomposition that computes monthly actives instead

task: Provision a new client workspace via Calendar + Notion
user_request: Onboard client Acme: create their shared calendar, a Notion workspace page, and link the kickoff event to the Notion page.
agent_action: Agent planned to create the kickoff calendar event with a description linking to the Notion page first, then create the Notion page — so the event description embedded a placeholder/guessed Notion URL that didn't resolve, and the cross-link was dead.
failure_type: Cross-link authored before the link target existed
root_cause: The plan created the event referencing a Notion page URL before that page was created, so the embedded link pointed at a non-existent or guessed id.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the Notion page URL is predictable and can be embedded before creation. Wrong because the page id is only known after creation. Avoidable by creating the Notion page first, capturing its real URL, then creating the calendar event with that URL in the description.
impact: The kickoff invite contained a dead Notion link; the client clicked through to a 404 before it was fixed.
correct_action: Create the Notion workspace page first, capture its real URL, then create the kickoff event with that verified URL embedded in the description.
recovery_plan: Open the kickoff event and confirm the dead link
Create the Notion workspace page and capture its URL
Patch the event description with the real URL via update_event
Verify the link resolves
Notify the client the link is fixed
evaluation_criteria: Checks the Notion page existed before the event linked to it
Verifies the embedded URL was a real captured id
Flags a cross-link authored before its target existed

task: Set up CRM-to-warehouse sync for new deals
user_request: Sync closed-won Salesforce opportunities into the warehouse fct_deals table nightly.
agent_action: Agent planned to schedule the warehouse MERGE job at 01:00 and the Salesforce extract job at 02:00, so every night the MERGE ran an hour before fresh data landed and fct_deals always reflected the previous day, perpetually one cycle stale.
failure_type: Downstream load scheduled before its upstream extract
root_cause: The plan scheduled the consuming MERGE earlier than the producing extract, inverting the data-dependency order in the orchestration schedule.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the two jobs are independent and ordering by clock time is fine. Wrong because the MERGE depends on the extract's output, so running it first always consumed stale data. Avoidable by expressing a dependency edge (extract → MERGE) in the orchestrator rather than wall-clock times that invert the order.
impact: fct_deals was perpetually one day behind, and a revenue dashboard understated closed-won deals each morning.
correct_action: Model the extract job as an upstream dependency of the MERGE in the orchestrator so the MERGE only runs after the extract completes, not on a fixed earlier clock time.
recovery_plan: Compare fct_deals max(close_date) against Salesforce to confirm the lag
Add a dependency edge: extract task → MERGE task
Remove the conflicting fixed-time schedules
Trigger a manual run to catch up
Verify fct_deals reflects today's closed-won deals
evaluation_criteria: Checks the load depended on the extract rather than a fixed earlier time
Verifies the dependency was expressed as an edge, not clock ordering
Flags a downstream job scheduled before its upstream

task: Roll out a feature behind a Notion-tracked checklist
user_request: Mark the 'Search v2' launch checklist complete and flip the feature flag, but only after every checklist item is done.
agent_action: Agent planned to flip the launch flag and then iterate the Notion checklist marking items done, so it enabled Search v2 in production before verifying the checklist's QA and rollback items were actually complete, violating the user's explicit gating condition.
failure_type: Gated action planned before its gating check
root_cause: The plan executed the flag flip before evaluating the checklist completion that was specified as a precondition, inverting the gate-then-act ordering.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the checklist was a formality that could be ticked after launch. Wrong because the user made checklist completion a hard precondition and two QA items were still open. Avoidable by querying the checklist, asserting all items checked, and only then flipping the flag.
impact: Search v2 went live with open QA items, exposing an unverified search ranking change to all users until it was rolled back.
correct_action: Query the Notion checklist, confirm every item is checked, and only then flip the feature flag; if any item is open, stop and report which ones.
recovery_plan: Query the Notion checklist for incomplete items

Complete the outstanding QA and rollback items

Re-flip the flag only after the gate passes

task: Hotfix release for a critical iOS crash
user_request: Ship a hotfix 4.7.1 for the login crash to the App Store as fast as possible.
agent_action: Agent planned to submit the build for App Store review and request expedited review first, then run the test suite and the dSYM upload afterward; the unrun tests would have caught that the hotfix branch was cut from main (which still had the crash) rather than the release/4.7 tag, so it shipped a build that didn't contain the fix.
failure_type: Submit-for-review planned before verification of the fix
root_cause: The plan placed App Store submission ahead of the test/verification and correct-branch checks that establish the hotfix actually contains the fix, so an unfixed build was submitted.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the hotfix branch already contained the fix and tests/verification could follow submission. Wrong because the branch was cut from main, not release/4.7, so the crash persisted; tests would have caught it. Avoidable by branching from the release tag, running the crash regression test green, then submitting.
impact: A hotfix that still contained the login crash was submitted for expedited review, risking shipping a non-fix to all users and burning the expedited-review slot.
correct_action: Branch the hotfix from the release/4.7 tag, run the login-crash regression test to green, upload dSYMs, and only then submit 4.7.1 for expedited review.
recovery_plan: Halt or withdraw the App Store submission before approval
Confirm the hotfix branch's base and that the crash reproduces
Re-cut the hotfix from the release/4.7 tag
Run the crash regression suite to green and upload dSYMs
Re-submit the verified 4.7.1 for expedited review
evaluation_criteria: Checks the fix was verified (correct base branch + passing test) before submission
Verifies submission did not precede the regression test
Flags a release submitted before the fix was confirmed present

task: Add canary routing rules to nginx
user_request: Send 5% of /checkout traffic to checkout-canary and the rest to checkout-stable.
agent_action: Agent planned to add a `split_clients` map referencing an `$upstream` variable inside a location block and reference upstream blocks it had not yet defined, ordering the location/map directives before the upstream{} definitions, so the config referenced undefined upstreams and failed to load.
failure_type: Upstream references planned before upstream blocks defined
root_cause: The plan referenced checkout-canary/checkout-stable upstreams in the routing logic before declaring the upstream{} blocks, so name resolution failed at config parse.
why_it_failed: Assumption: split_clients and proxy_pass can reference upstreams defined later or implicitly. Wrong because nginx requires upstream{} blocks to be declared (in http context) before they're referenced. Avoidable by defining both upstream blocks first, then the split_clients map, then proxy_pass, validating with nginx -t.
impact: `nginx -t` failed on undefined upstreams; the canary rollout was blocked until the config order was corrected.
correct_action: Define the checkout-canary and checkout-stable upstream blocks, add the split_clients map to a routing variable, set proxy_pass to that variable, then validate with nginx -t before reload.
recovery_plan: Run nginx -t to capture the undefined-upstream error
Add the upstream{} blocks for canary and stable
Define the split_clients 5/95 map
Point proxy_pass at the split variable
Validate with nginx -t and reload
evaluation_criteria: Checks upstream blocks were defined before being referenced
Verifies nginx -t passed before reload
Flags references to undefined upstreams in the plan

task: Deduplicate contacts before a HubSpot import
user_request: Import the new lead list but don't create duplicates of existing contacts.
agent_action: Agent planned to run the CSV import via the batch-create endpoint first and run a dedupe merge pass afterward, so it created duplicate contact records for everyone already in the CRM and then attempted to merge thousands of pairs, some of which had already triggered duplicate workflow enrollments.
failure_type: Import planned before dedupe instead of upsert
root_cause: The plan chose create-then-merge rather than an email-keyed upsert, guaranteeing duplicate creation before any dedupe could run.
why_it_failed: Assumption: duplicates can be cleaned up after a bulk create. Wrong because create-first generates duplicates that fire workflows and pollute reports, and merging is lossy and incomplete. Avoidable by upserting on the email unique key (or searching existing contacts first) so no duplicate is ever created.
impact: Thousands of duplicate contacts were created, triggering spurious workflow enrollments and skewing contact counts until a costly merge cleanup.
correct_action: Use the email-keyed upsert (batch upsert with idProperty=email) or search existing contacts first, so the import updates matches and only creates genuinely new leads.
recovery_plan: Identify duplicate contact pairs by email
Suspend workflows that enrolled the duplicates
Merge or delete the duplicate records
Re-import remaining leads with email-keyed upsert
Verify contact counts and workflow enrollments are correct
evaluation_criteria: Checks an upsert/search-first strategy was used instead of create-then-merge
Verifies no duplicate creation preceded dedupe
Flags a create-before-dedupe plan

task: Archive old calendars before a workspace cleanup
user_request: Clean up our shared calendars: remove the deprecated 'Old Team' calendar but keep its historical events accessible.
agent_action: Agent planned to delete the 'Old Team' calendar and then export its events to a backup, so once the calendar was deleted via calendars.delete the events were gone and the export step had nothing to read, losing the history the user explicitly wanted kept.
failure_type: Delete planned before the export that depends on it
root_cause: The plan ordered the irreversible delete before the export that needed the calendar to still exist, so the dependency that preserved history was destroyed first.
why_it_failed: Assumption: events can be exported from a deleted calendar or recovered later. Wrong because calendars.delete is irreversible and removes all events immediately. Avoidable by exporting all events (events.list with pagination) to a backup, verifying the export, then deleting the calendar.
impact: Historical events from 'Old Team' were permanently deleted before backup, losing records the user wanted preserved.
correct_action: List and export all events from the 'Old Team' calendar to a backup, verify the export is complete, then delete the calendar.
recovery_plan: Attempt recovery via admin/Vault if within the retention window
List and export any recoverable events to backup
Verify the backup completeness against expected counts
Only delete the calendar after a verified export exists
Document the data-loss window and notify the user
evaluation_criteria: Checks events were exported and verified before deletion
Verifies the irreversible delete ran last
Flags a destructive step ordered before its dependent backup

task: Stand up nginx with Let's Encrypt before DNS cutover
user_request: Issue a TLS cert for shop.example.com and serve it, we'll point DNS at this box.
agent_action: Agent planned to run certbot to issue the cert using the HTTP-01 challenge before the shop.example.com DNS record pointed at the server, so the challenge validation failed (Let's Encrypt couldn't reach the domain) and after several failed attempts the plan hit the ACME rate limit.
failure_type: Cert issuance planned before DNS resolved to the host
root_cause: The plan ran the HTTP-01 ACME challenge, which requires the domain to resolve to the issuing server, before the DNS A record was pointed at the box, so validation could not succeed.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a cert can be issued any time regardless of DNS. Wrong because HTTP-01 needs the domain to resolve to this server so the challenge file is reachable; DNS still pointed elsewhere. Avoidable by either cutting DNS over first, or using the DNS-01 challenge, and checking resolution with dig before invoking certbot.
impact: Repeated failed validations consumed the Let's Encrypt failed-validation rate limit, blocking issuance for an hour even after DNS was fixed.
correct_action: Confirm shop.example.com resolves to this host (or use the DNS-01 challenge), then run certbot once with a verified reachable challenge path.
recovery_plan: Run dig shop.example.com to confirm where it resolves
Either cut DNS to this host or switch to the DNS-01 challenge
Wait out the ACME rate-limit window
Run certbot once with the verified challenge method
Confirm the cert installs and nginx serves it
evaluation_criteria: Checks DNS resolution (or DNS-01) was verified before issuance
Verifies certbot was not run against an unresolvable domain
Flags repeated issuance attempts hitting the rate limit
